title: Active-o3: Giving MLLMs the Ability to Choose Where to Look
one_liner: Teach a vision-language model to pick smart regions of an image to zoom in on, using reward-based training, so it wastes less effort on irrelevant areas.
lead: Imagine a person looking at a busy photograph. They don't study every inch equally — they pick out the important bits and focus hard there. Most vision-language models (computer programs that read both images and text) don't do this; they process the whole image at once, wasting time on distracting details. Active-o3 teaches them to learn where to look, by rewarding them for picking regions that actually matter for the task.

problem.h2: The problem: models look everywhere equally
paras: Vision-language models (programs that understand both images and text together) process a whole image at once. If a photo has a tiny object buried in a crowd, the model reads millions of pixels of background noise before it ever focuses on the target. That wastes time and fails on crowded scenes. A human would zoom in on the promising region first.

A beginner might try: show the model the whole image once, then ask it to describe what it sees. But it gets lost in detail. Or hand-code which regions matter (write rules saying zoom in on faces, or cars). But that breaks the moment the task changes. What we need: let the model learn by experience which regions to zoom into, the same way humans learned to scan photos efficiently.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Use reward-based training (giving points for good choices) to teach a vision-language model to decide which image regions to zoom in on and examine closely, without anyone telling it the answer.

panels.title: 1. The full image arrives
panels.caption: Model reads the entire noisy photo at once, wastes effort.

panels.title: 2. The model makes a guess

panels.caption: Model chooses which region to zoom into next.

steps.text: Model gets the whole cluttered photo as input.
Internal logic picks a candidate region to zoom into (coordinates and zoom level).
Model processes just that region in detail, avoiding distraction from the rest.
Check whether the zoomed patch contains the information needed to solve the task (object found or not).
Training algorithm strengthens the region-picking logic when rewards are high, weakens it when rewards are low.

object.h2: What the paper changes: region selection decisions
paras: The paper does not change the core vision-language model itself (that stays the same). Instead, it adds a new trainable decision-making layer that picks which regions to zoom into, and fine-tunes that layer to maximize rewards.

hidden.name: how much task-relevant information a region contains
paras: The paper measures something new: which image regions actually carry the information you need to solve the task (find the small object, read the distant sign, etc.). A region with the target object is high-informativeness; a region of blank sky is low-informativeness.

The paper estimates this by asking: after the model zooms into this region, does it get the answer right? High accuracy on a region means that region was informative; low accuracy means it was not. The training process uses this signal (reward for good regions, penalty for wasteful ones) to teach the model's selection logic.

heat.caption: Darker means the region gives more task-relevant information. Borders mark top informativeness.

reads.html: Informativeness is just how much useful information a region has for your specific task. Finding a person in a crowd means a region with the person's face is highly informative; a region of empty stadium is not.

The paper learns informativeness implicitly through reward: high reward when the model's choice leads to correct answers, low reward when it leads to mistakes or wasted computation, because the training algorithm strengthens choices that earned high scores and weakens ones that earned low scores. Over many training steps, the model discovers which types of regions pay off.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: reward teaches smart region choices
paras: The core mechanism is simple. Start with a model that picks regions randomly (no skill). Every time it picks a good region (one that helps solve the task), give it a big reward, because that region contained information needed to get the answer right. Every time it picks a bad region (wastes compute, finds nothing), give it a small reward or a penalty, because that region wasted resources without helping. The training algorithm nudges the region-selection logic to repeat the high-reward choices and avoid the low-reward ones, because mathematically the learning rule updates in the direction of higher rewards. This mirrors the way a child learns to reach for red apples after tasting sweet ones.

Why does this work? Because the task itself encodes what matters. If the task is to find a tiny insect in a photo, the model quickly learns that zooming into the green plant region pays off (reward comes back high), but zooming into sky does not. The model never sees a rule saying zoom at plants; it discovered that pattern from reward. This works on any task: object detection, reading text from a distance, autonomous driving — the reward signal always points the model toward informative regions because the task outcome is the ground truth.

stages.s: Full image + task (find small object, read sign, etc.)
Region selector proposes candidate zoom area
Task checker: does this region have the answer?
Reward signal: 1.0 if yes, 0.1 if no
Region selector learns to repeat high-reward choices

math.h2: Equation: weighted reward for region choices
math.words: Total training reward is the sum of task-solved-correctly reward plus efficiency reward (time spent), weighted to balance finding the answer fast.
math.equation: R = w_task * reward_task(region) + w_eff * reward_efficiency(region) where reward_task is 1.0 if answer correct, 0.0 otherwise, and reward_efficiency penalizes unused computation.
symbols: total reward for this region choice
did zooming this region lead to the right answer (1.0 yes, 0.0 no)
penalty for wasted computation time (larger penalty for regions that took long but failed)
how much we care about getting the right answer
how much we care about being fast (not wasting tokens on irrelevant regions)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Region A: found the target insect, took 4 tokens. reward_task = 1.0, reward_efficiency = 0.9 (fast). R = 0.8 * 1.0 + 0.2 * 0.9 = 0.98 (strong reward).
Region B: found nothing useful, took 2 tokens. reward_task = 0.0, reward_efficiency = 0.95 (very fast but pointless). R = 0.8 * 0.0 + 0.2 * 0.95 = 0.19 (weak reward).
Region C: found nothing, took 6 tokens. reward_task = 0.0, reward_efficiency = 0.3 (slow waste). R = 0.8 * 0.0 + 0.2 * 0.3 = 0.06 (tiny reward).
Training learns to pick regions like A (high reward) and avoid regions like C (waste of time).

math.note: The two-part reward (correctness plus speed) mirrors how humans learn to scan: we zoom into promising regions fast, and ignore distracting areas entirely.

bars.h2: Comparison: model with and without active perception

charts.title: Old approach: look at everything equally
charts.note: Model processes the whole image, wasting effort on irrelevant pixels. Misses small objects in clutter.

charts.title: With Active-o3 learning where to zoom
charts.note: Model learned to zoom into promising regions first. Gets higher accuracy because zoomed regions contain the target clearly without background noise, and uses fewer tokens because it skips irrelevant areas entirely. (Illustrative teaching numbers; see paper for real benchmarks.)

items.b: Reward signal is weak or ambiguous.
items.html: If the task itself is unclear (maybe the target object is borderline visible), the model receives mixed rewards (sometimes 1.0, sometimes 0.0 from similar regions). Training becomes noisy and slow. The model cannot learn a clear strategy.

items.b: Regions are too coarse or too fine.
items.html: If the model can only zoom into huge chunks, it still sees lots of clutter. If regions are tiny pixels, it misses context. The zoom granularity must fit the task; the paper finds this through ablation.

items.b: Model overfits to specific benchmark regions.
items.html: If training only shows objects in the center, the model learns to zoom center. Then on a real photo with an object in the corner, it fails. Reward training requires diverse data.

items.b: Done right: use task-derived reward on realistic data.
items.html: Train on a variety of images and target locations. Let the reward signal (whether the zoomed region helped or not) be the sole teacher. The model generalizes to new images because it learned the underlying principle: informative regions help, uninformative ones do not.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small interactive example: load a photo with one or more small objects (a toy doll in a living room, a street sign far away). Train a model with Active-o3 for a few steps, starting from random region selection. Plot how the model's chosen regions shift over time: early on, random scattered regions; after a few training steps, the zoomed regions cluster around the actual target. Show the model's accuracy on that photo improving as better regions are selected, because when the model picks regions containing the target, the vision model can read it clearly and answer correctly, but when it picks background regions, vision fails. Poor accuracy initially because the region selector picks randomly and gets background; accuracy climbs as region selection improves toward the real target, because the training algorithm strengthens region choices that led to high reward (target found).
demo.metric_eq: Accuracy on task = number of correct answers after zooming / total number of zoom attempts. Show this rising as region selection improves.
demo.closing: The demo should make impossible to miss: the model learned which regions matter purely from reward signal, without any hand-written rule saying where to look.
